title: The priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
hook: the Lord bless you and keep you, make his face shine on you
carry: the lord bless you and keep you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jubilee, a ram's horn, land returned and people sent home free. Your line: proclaim liberty.

In burial caves just outside Jerusalem, archaeologists found two tiny rolled-up scrolls of silver, each small enough to hide in your palm, so fragile that unrolling them took great care. Scratched into the silver were a few lines of Hebrew. Someone had worn them, perhaps as amulets, maybe around the neck. And the words inside were a blessing, the same one churches and synagogues still speak today. Three lines people have been carrying close ever since.
screen: `TWO SILVER SCROLLS IN A TOMB.` → `SMALL ENOUGH TO WEAR.` → `THE WORDS INSIDE: A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: In the book of Numbers, God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people. Then the words, in the King James Bible: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Three lines, and they grow. In Hebrew the first line is three words, the second five, the third seven, like a wave building. Each line names the LORD and gives two gifts. Bless and keep: provide for you and guard you. Shine and be gracious: a face lighting up when it sees you, the way a grandparent's does when you walk in. Lift up his countenance: turn toward you, look right at you. And the last word, the one everything builds to, is shalom: peace, wholeness, nothing missing. Notice it's thee, singular. The blessing is spoken to the whole people, but every you is a single you. A crowd, blessed one person at a time. Then God says why: "they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The priests speak the words. God does the blessing. In synagogues it can be said by the kohanim, families who trace their line to the priests. Churches use it too: some ministers and priests raise their hands and say it at the end of a service, at a wedding, over a newborn, at a grave.
screen: `THREE LINES: THREE, FIVE, SEVEN WORDS.` · `A FACE THAT LIGHTS UP.` · `ENDING IN SHALOM.` · `PRIESTS SPEAK, GOD BLESSES.` · then, large: `THE LORD MAKE HIS FACE SHINE UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person, someone you love, someone you worry about, or someone you find hard, and see their face. Then say the old words over them slowly, one line per breath: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee. The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. If those words aren't yours, simply hold them in mind and wish them well.
Shalom. Hebrew for peace, wholeness, nothing missing: the last word of the priestly blessing, building like a wave from bless to peace.
Your line: the lord bless you and keep you. People have carried those words close for a very long time. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some pastors and priests say the Aaronic blessing at the end of worship with raised hands, and it is spoken at some weddings, baptisms and funerals; in synagogues, kohanim may say it over the congregation.

chat.says: Where does that blessing about the Lord's face shining come from?
options: Numbers 6: God gave it to Aaron's sons to speak, and says he does the blessing.
It's from a psalm David wrote for his son Solomon's coronation day.
It's a medieval church prayer that later got added to the Bible.
chat.meaning: The priestly blessing is in Numbers 6. Aaron's sons speak the three lines, and God says, I will bless them.

Aaron.meaning: Moses' brother, the first high priest

shalom.meaning: Hebrew for peace, wholeness, nothing missing

kohanim.meaning: Jewish families who trace their line to the priests

countenance.meaning: face; to lift it up is to look right at you

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook stripped of the date (1979), 'took years', 'among the oldest pieces of biblical text ever found', 'centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'more than two and a half thousand years' (dates, counts and superlatives the cited text does not give), in voice, screen, myth and trapdoor; 'in churches it's used everywhere: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant' narrowed (the Aaronic blessing is not a standard Orthodox dismissal) to 'some ministers and priests'. The 3/5/7 Hebrew word count is kept because it can be read off the text; Keeper to confirm.

Ketef Hinnom scrolls: found 1979 by Gabriel Barkay; dated to the late seventh or early sixth century BC; unrolled and read over following years. The script says 'more than two and a half thousand years'. Confirm.
Word counts 3/5/7 in the Hebrew of 6:24–26 (counting YHWH as a word); confirm.
Original: יְבָרֶכְךָ is the first word of the blessing (before YHWH); confirm. Pronunciation 'ye-va-re-KHE-kha'; check stress.
Practice invites the listener to say the KJV words over someone, offered as optional; it quotes scripture rather than writing a prayer.
